newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey Islamists threaten polls in row with army.
newsitem.headline: Turkey Islamists threaten polls in row with army.

text.p: Turkey's ruling Islamists on Friday countered the army's demands for a clampdown on religious activism with a threat of new elections to strengthen the government's hand against the secularist generals.

But the call for early polls by a close aide of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan was seen by politicians as a scare tactic and received little backing. Coalition partner Tansu Ciller ruled out balloting.

"At a time when Turkey is choked, the democratic system is being squeezed and pressure is mounting, we have to go to elections. That is my personal opinion " the Milliyet newspaper quoted State Minister Abdullah Gul as saying.
The secularist military told the government last week to stamp out Islamist zeal. Erbakan made clear he resented the order as an unsubtle attempt to weaken him and his supporters.
Other parties have ignored Islamist pleas for parliamentary solidarity against the generals, forcing Erbakan to reluctantly approve a military statement urging the crackdown.
It is far from clear, however, that he would implement what is in effect an assault on his own core constituency.

Deputy Prime Minister Ciller, a pro-Western conservative who often sits uneasily with the Islamists, said there would be no polls. "There will be no such thing. The government will continue," she told reporters in Istanbul.
Welfare, with 160 MPs in the 550-seat assembly, would need the backing of another major faction in parliament to force elections.
MPs from across the political spectrum say privately they are reluctant to go to the polls in fear of losing financial perks which can only be claimed after two years in parliament.
Erbakan's well-organised Welfare Party formed an alliance with Ciller's True Path after narrowly winning general polls in 1995 with 21 percent of the vote.
Some predictions since then have put Islamist support as high as 30 percent but analysts doubt Welfare could win enough seats to mould Turkey into a strict Islamic state like Iran.

The army row has cast a shadow over recent privatisation successes key to Erbakan's bid to balance the 1997 budget. He has also let down his many Kurdish voters by not living up to a promise to solve a rebel conflict through Moslem brotherhood.

Istanbul stocks, highly sensitive to Turkey's many political twists, dived 3.71 percent in morning trading. The market had already lost eight percent of its value in the first four days of this week because of the instability.

Minister Gul suggested the possibility of the Islamists coming out of fresh elections with a greater majority would force the military to back down. "When it comes to giving an account to the people the soldiers' attitude will change."
"In a situation like this it is best to go the people," said Gul, regarded as the architect of Erbakan's bid to take NATO member Turkey closer to its Moslem neighbours.
Visits by the prime minister to Iran and Libya last year angered Turkey's secularists and Ankara's close ally Washington.
Erbakan is the first Islamist to lead the Turks since the collapse of the Ottoman Empire in the 1920s.
He was due to meet parliamentary speaker Mustafa Kalemli for talks on a government call for an unprecedented debate in the national assembly on the military's anti-Islamist demands.
Turkish cabinets usually take monthly military recommendations on board with little argument.
